events.event_narrative: Four inches of snow was reported at the Pecos airport.
Four to six inches of snow was reported in Stanton.
Four inches of snow was reported in Big Lake.
Four to five inches of snow was reported in Odessa.
Four inches of snow was reported in Andrews.
Four inches of snow was reported 17 miles northeast of Gail.
Three to five inches of snow was reported in and around Tatum.
Four inches of snow was reported at Artesia and Hope.
Four inches of snow was reported 4 miles west of Fort Davis.
Four inches of snow was reported in Tatum.

Northeast winds of 40 mph or greater persisted through Guadalupe Pass for nearly 18 hours.   Although no gusts of 58 mph or higher occurred, sustained winds ranged from 40 to 48 mph for most of the mentioned period.
Aside from the one gust to 59 mph at 1351 LST on February 22nd, sustained winds of 40 to 46 mph occurred through Guadalupe Pass for several hours on both February 21st and 22nd.
Gusts of 75 and 65 mph occurred at McDonald Observatory at 410 and 635 LST respectively.
Several gusts over 58 mph occurred at the Guadalupe Peak Raws site, the highest of which was 65 mph that occurred at 0400 LST.
Sustained winds of 40 to 46 mph occurred through Guadalupe Pass for several hours.
A 59 mph gust occurred at the Guadalupe Peak RAWS site.
Several gusts over 64 mph occurred at McDonald Observatory with the highest gust of 92 mph occurring at 1640 LST.
The hail covered the ground and a few 6 inch drifts were present.

Significant hail damage was observed at car dealerships located north of Church Street in Carlsbad.  Although there were specific reports of roof damage, an exact number of homes impacted could not be established and this portion of the property damage was roughly estimated.
The Caverns City Airport ASOS recorded sustained winds of 40 mph or greater for two hours, and a gust to 54 mph at 1453 LST.
The Caverns City Airport ASOS had a gust of 58 mph.
An extended period of strong winds occurred in the Guadalupe Mountains, with several gusts over 70 mph recorded.
An extended period of high winds occurred in the lower elevations of the Guadalupe Mountains. The highest of which was 66 mph.
A period of high winds occurred in the Davis Mountains with several gusts over 60 mph, including a gust to 74 mph.
Many gusts over 60 mph occurred with a couple of gusts over 70 mph.
Gusts over 60 mph were common with a couple of gusts over 80 mph.
A few gusts over 60 mph occurred, with 77 mph being the highest.
Several windows, roofs and other structural items were damaged at the Gage Hotel in Marathon, TX.
A park ranger reported a 3 foot boulder was blocking SH 54 due to high flowing water.  Low water crossings were also impassable.
A metal roof was blown off a structure due to a strong wind gust, estimated to be near 60 mph.
More than 6 inches of flowing water was present across several low water crossings along Route 16 from Castolon to Santa Elena Canyon.  There was no significant damage reported.
Six to eight inches of flowing water covered the intersection of Interstate 20 and County Road 1140.  There were no reports of damage.
Gusts over 60 mph occurred almost non-stop in the higher elevations of the Guadalupe Mountains on 4/6/10.  A couple of gusts over 70 mph occurred during this time also.
Nearly constant high winds occurred through Guadalupe Pass with several gusts over 60 mph, and a maximum gust of 71 mph at 0651 MST.

An extended period of gusts over 60 mph was observed throughout the day.  The strongest gust occurred at 1350 MST, which was 69 mph.  Several structures were damaged by the winds including a chimney chase, home siding, a wooden fence, and 3 barns.  The roofs and siding on the barns were blown off.
An extended period of high winds occurred in the higher elevations of the Guadalupe Mountains with gusts almost constantly over 60 mph and one as high as 83 mph.
Several gusts over 60 mph were recorded at McDonald Observatory, along with a 72 mph gust at 0440 CST.
Perodic strong winds occurred in Guadalupe Pass from May 6th to May 8th.  The highest gust was 59 mph at 1751 LST on May 6th.
High winds occurred in the higher elevations of the Guadalupe Mountains.
Several gusts between 60 and 70 mph occured during this time at McDonald Observatory, with a gust to 81 mph at 1420 CST.
A 67 mph gust was recorded at the Alpine Casparis Municipal Airport.
The wind gusts during this time averaged 65 mph, although the strongest gust recorded was 76 mph at 1950 CST.
Damage was not reported with the wind gust.
The hail caused major damage to a trailer home, destroying windows, siding and the entire skirt.
A wind gust blew over an aluminum carport and twisted it.
Several large tree limbs were snapped by the wind gust.
Several power poles were knocked down/snapped by the wind gust.  The time of this report was estimated according to radar data.
Eight power poles were knocked over/snapped by the wind gust.
Damage was not reported with this wind gust.

A high water rescue was executed along Armstrong Road near Walnut Arroyo.  The man was washed downstream 300 yards.  The rescue attempt was successful. No injuries were reported with this event, and the damage estimate was based on damage done to the vehicle.
At 4:45 PM MST, the public reported 12 to 18 inches of flowing water across their driveway and street in front of their home.  The flood waters destroyed around 7 acres of alfalfa crop.
Several windows and skylights were broken by the hail on one home.  In addition, two more homes received roof and window damage.  One vehicle also reported damage.

At 1536 CST, a tornado was confirmed by trained spotters about 22 miles west of Fort Stockton.  The tornado then tracked south southeast for about 4 minutes, and was spotted by local law enforcement.  It was determined by a damage survey, and several spotter reports, that the tornado dissipated around 1549 CST.  Only minor damage was done to vegetation by this tornado.  Please see the photos of the tornado taken by the spotters.
A trained weather spotter reported a tornado at 1715 CST about 18 miles west southwest of Fort Stockton.  No damage was reported with this weak brief touchdown.

A spotter report from a NWS employee and a damage survey both determined that at approximately 1756 CST, a tornado developed about 11 miles southeast of Verhalen, TX.  It then moved southeastward damaging a total of 12 powers poles.  All but two of these poles were broken into 3 or 4 pieces each.  The broken poles were indicative of EF-2 type damage.  At 1802 CST, a Pecos County Sherriff���s Deputy took a photo of the tornado near the Pecos and Reeves County line.  Finally, at 1806 CST the NWS employee captured the tornado in its dissipating stage.
No known damage was reported with this gust.
The wind gust snapped large tree limbs.
Several windows on a home were broken by the hail, but no known specifics were given with regards to replacement costs.
A strong wind gust blew off the metal roof of a storage structure.

A brief tornado developed near a residence, doing minor damage.  The time of the tornado's formation was estimated from radar and the storm report from the owner of the home.  At approximately 17:35 pm CST, the tornado blew an old telephone antenna a couple hundred yards away.  It then blew a stack of wooden pallets 15 to 20 yards away.  In addition, several 5 inch limbs were broken off of trees.  The tornado lasted less than 2 minutes.

Members of the Vortex2 team and TWISTEX both confirmed a rope tornado at 11:56 AM CST approximately 17 miles east southeast of Kermit, TX.  The tornado then moved east northeast into western Ector County, with a confirmed dissipation time of 12:04 PM CST.  There was no significant damage reported with this tornado.

At 12:15 pm CST, members of the TWISTEX research group confirmed the formation of a tornado approximately 6.5 miles south of Notrees.  This tornado progressed northeastward around 20 mph, first causing damage to power poles around from 12:16 to 12:17 pm CST.  As it continued to track to the northeast, the tornado caused significant damage to oil equipment from 12:19 to 12:22 pm CST.  Two type 320 pump jacks, each weighing 71,000 pounds including the concrete base, were blown over.  The tornado then began to weaken at 12:27 pm CST, and dissipated at 12:28 pm CST approximately 2 miles southeast of Notrees, TX.

At 12:32 pm CST, members of the TWISTEX research team confirmed a rope tornado approximately 5.5 miles south southeast of Goldsmith, TX, and north of Highway 302.  The tornado then moved northeast a little over a mile where it dissipated at 12:36 pm CST.  No significant damage was observed with this tornado.

At 13:46 pm CST, local law enforcement reported that a car had been swept into the Scharbauer Draw near Jackson Street and Scharbauer Drive.  When emergency officials arrived on the scene, they were unable to locate the car.  Later that evening, a wrecker service was removing the reemerged car from the water when they found the body of a female driver inside.  Numerous cars were submerged throughout Midland, and several high water rescues were executed.  The police received over 92 submerged vehicle reports, although some may have been repeats.  The monetary damage for this event was estimated based on the number of vehicles observed under water.

At 1520 pm CST, the Howard County Emergency Manager reported flash flooding in and around Big Spring, TX.  Fifty-five gallon drums were floating down roadways and several motorists were stranded in vehicles submerged under water.
A brief touchdown was reported by a trained spotter near Greenwood, TX.  The time of this report was estimated according to radar data.  No significant damage was reported with this tornado.
Several homes, vehicles and tractors had their windows broken by the hail.  In addition, damage was also done to roofs and siding on homes.
A window was blown out at the Brantley Lake State Park office building.  The winds were estimated to be near 75 mph.
A horse trailer was blown off the road, in addition to a power pole being snapped and a yield sign being damaged at the intersection of SH 137 and US 285.
This gust was measured by a Weather Underground weather station.
A NWS Employee reported 6-9 inches of flowing water at the intersection of Eisenhower and Anetta in Midland, TX.  Several cars were stranded across Midland due to high water.
The police department barraceded low water crossings within Big Spring, Tx.  A few morotists were stranded in 12 to 18 inches of water.

The Texas Department of Transportation reported a road closure due to high water across US 80 and Loop 338 in Odessa, TX.  Another report of flash flooding was received from the news media near Highway 80 on the south side of Odessa.
A trained spotter reported 6 inches of flowing water near the intersection of FMR 1787 and US 385.
The public reported 2 feet of water over the intersection of SH 137 and US 285, about 18 miles west northwest of Carlsbad, NM.
A small barn was blow over about 5 miles southeast of Artesia.

A land owner reported that a 4 foot tree was blown over and several 4 to 5 inch tree limbs were broken.  In addition, the roof of a 30' by 50' barn was torn off and some of the home's roof shingles were damaged.
A 60 mph wind gust was estimated by a storm spotter in Shafter.  No damage was reported with this gust.

Several side roll irrigation sprinklers were destroyed by a strong wind gust in Atoka, NM.  The time of this report was estimated according to radar and another wind gust recorded by the Artesia ASOS.
The Reeves County Emergency Manager reported that an old trailer was blown over at approximately 7 PM CST in the city of Pecos, TX.  A girl was injured when the trailer fell on top of her.
Law enforcement reported powerlines were downed by strong winds in Andrews, TX.
The public reported an estimated gust near 60 mph.  No damage was reported with this gust.
The local law enforcement reported 3.5 to 4 feet of standing water along US 385, 24 miles south of Fort Stockton.  Several cars were stranded due to the high water.
The local law enforcement reported power lines down at the border patrol checkpoint.
Law enforcement closed a bridge due to high water in Rooney Park.
Local law enforcement reported two stalled vehicles in Odessa due to high water.

The media reported downed power lines in West Odessa.  In addition, a NWS damage survey conducted the following day revealed damage to several other structures including a trailer, two mobile homes, and several roofs.
An 82 mph wind gust damaged two hangars at the Pecos County Airport.  It also destroyed several trees on the aiport's property.
The local law enforcement estimated a wind gust to be near 70 mph.  No damage was reported with this gust.

A trained spotter took a photo of a short lived rope tornado near the city of Lamesa, TX.  The tornado's track, duration and approximate position were all estimated according to radar data.  No damage was reported with this weak tornado.
The local law enforcement in Lamesa, TX reported cars were stranded along several roads.  The water was estimated to be 2 feet deep.
The Gaines County Emergency Manager reported water running over US Highway 83 about 5 miles east of Seagraves.  The depth of the water was not reported.
At 510 AM CST, a COOP observer reported significant flooding in and around Sheffield, TX.  Highway 349 just south of Sheffield was impassable and closed due to high water.
Over 1 foot of standing water was present on the Sanderson High School football field.  Several roadways were also closed due to high water throughout Sanderson, TX.
A local gas station reported flooding across McCamey, TX.  The water was high enough to move into both the middle school and elementary school.

The Carlsbad, NM Police Department reported high water across southern portions of the city.  Several streets were impassable, with the water covering the hood of one car.  Most streets within southern Carlsbad were blockaded by law enforcement.

At 2005 CST, a spotter first reported 6 to 8 inches of flowing water over portions of SH 137, just north of SH 176, in Martin County.  Water was also running over FM 846 east of SH 137.  About an hour later, TXDOT closed SH 176 in Martin County from near the Martin County line east to the Howard County line.   Several motorists were stranded in high water along the highway.
Several motorists were stranded in high water within the city of Pecos, TX.
Several streets in Fort Stockton were impassable due to high water.  State Highway 18 from Fort Stockton north to the county line also had water flowing across it.

Several roadways were flooded within and near the city of McCamey, TX.  Six inches of water was reported to be running over many streets in McCamey.  Some roadways, including State Highway 67, had at least 1 foot of flowing water over them.  Near the end of the event, 2 feet of flowing water was reported on King Mountain Road 5 miles northeast of McCamey.
Heavy rain occured across Eddy county with 2.5 to 3 feet of flowing water across Dark canyon road and Hidalgo road.  This contributed to a high water rescue.
Heavy rain caused flooding in northern Culberson county.  This flooding took place 16 miles south of whites City where arroyos and streams were flooded as well as low water crossings.
Heavy rain fell across Mitchell County with 18 inches of flowing water across portions of SH 208 south of FM 644.
Flash flooding was observed by trained spotters in and around the city of Midland, TX.  Water was flowing over the curbs at several locations.

Significant wind damage was observed within an area 5 miles southeast of Lamesa.  Several power poles were knocked over and damaged, trees were uprooted, a large barn and carport were destroyed, and a center pivot irrigation system was flipped over.

Several reports of downed power lines/poles were received across central and northwestern Dawson County.  The first report was near 4:02 PM CST in Punkin Center.  As the thunderstorm progressed southeastward, high winds were also reported in Lamesa where large trees were knocked down. The monetary damage was estimated for this event.
A trained spotter reported his flag was partially torn by the wind gust.  A 6 foot long tree branch was also found broken near State Highway 137.

At 4:10 PM MST, a trained weather spotter relayed a report of up to 1 1/2' of water on Mesa Street in Carlsbad.  A car was also stalled/flooded at the intersection of Blodgett and Mesquite Street.  Flooding continued almost through 9:00 PM MST across Carlsbad.  One foot of flowing water was reported to be flowing over Blodgett and Pate Streets at 8:40 PM MST.

Near 3:15 PM CST, the public reported a tornado near the end of Perry Avenue in Odessa, TX.  The tornado only lasted about one minute and there was no evidence of any significant damage, although some pump jacks and dumpsters were shaken about.  This tornado, and its size, was estimated to be an EF0 according to several public storm reports.
Hail was reported by the West Odessa volunteer fire department.
A severe storm produced quarter hail 5-10 miles north of Girvin on FM11.  The hail covered the road 1 inch deep.
Quarter sized hail occurred just west of the intersection of FM 3901 and SH 176.  Cotton crop damage was reported, but the acreage was unknown.
High winds occurred in the Guadalupe Mountains due to strong mid level winds at the base of a passing shortwave trough.
Sustained winds of 40 mph or greater funneled through Guadalupe Pass for several hours due to a passing shortwave trough, and strong mid level winds associated with it.
High winds occurred in the higher elevations of the Davis Mountains due to strong mid level winds over the area.
High winds occurred in the higher elevations of the Guadalupe Mountains due to strong mid level winds over the area.
Strong mid level winds mixed down into the higher elevations of the Guadalupe Mountains.
Funneled winds through Guadalupe Pass reached gusts of 58 and 59 mph as strong mid level winds persisted over the area.
Persistent strong mid level westerly winds resulted in a few hours of high winds in Guadalupe Pass.
Persistent strong westerly flow aloft resulted in high winds in portions of the Guadalupe Mountains.
High winds occurred in portions of the Guadalupe Mountains due to persistent strong mid level westerly flow over the area.
Westerly winds funneling through Guadalupe Pass resulted in high winds as westerly flow aloft continued to be strong over the area.
Westerly winds funneling through Guadalupe Pass resulted in high winds there due to strong mid level winds at the base of a passing upper level trough.
Strong winds occurred in the higher elevations of the Guadalupe Mountains due to strong mid level winds over the area at the base of a passing upper level trough.
High winds occurred in Guadalupe Pass as strong mid level winds over the area mixed down and funneled through the Pass.
Strong mid level winds over the area mixed down into the higher elevations of the Guadalupe Mountains.
A few high wind gusts occurred in the higher elevations of the Davis Mountains as a belt of stronger mid level winds sagged south across west Texas.

Several brief touchdowns were reported near Rankin, TX along US Highway 67.  The tornado only lasted about two minutes and did not produce any damage along its short path.  The path length and width of this tornado were estimated according to spotter reports.

A brief land spout tornado developed on the north end of Artesia, NM.  The exact location of this tornado was estimated according to the spotter's description.  No damage was done, and it only persisted for about 1 minute.
A brief land spout was observed southeast of Seminole, TX.  It only persisted for a minute or less, and did no damage.

Initially, strong westerly winds affected the Guadalupe Mountains due to strong mid level winds over the region at the base of a large upper trough.  After the arctic frontal boundary moved through the area in the wake of the upper trough, only the lower elevations of the Guadalupe Mountains were affected by sustained northeasterly winds of 40 mph or greater for several hours.
A brief thunderstorm combined with environmental windy conditions to produce a strong wind gust.
Sustained northeast winds of 40 mph or greater occurred for several hours.
Sustained northeast winds of 40 mph or greater occurred for nearly 24 hours in Guadalupe Pass.
Wind chill values of -15  to -20 degrees Fahrenheit occurred during much of a two day period in the Guadalupe Mountains.
Arctic air over the region combined with northeast winds and resulted in wind chill values of -15 to -20 degrees Fahrenheit at Mount Locke in the Davis Mountains.
The Queen RAWS had wind chills of -15 to -35 degrees Fahrenheit.
Batdraw RAWS had wind chills of -15 to -35 degrees Fahrenheit.
The Caprock RAWS had wind chills of -15 to -35 degrees Fahrenheit.
Carlsbad ASOS indicated wind chills of -15 to -20 degrees Fahrenheit for a few hours.
The Artesia AWOS indicated wind chills of -15 to-20 degrees Fahrenheit.
The Tatum West Texas Mesonet site indicated wind chills of -15 to -25 degrees Fahrenheit.
The Tatum West Texas Mesonet site indicated wind chills of -15 to -25 degrees Fahrenheit.
The Tatum West Texas Mesonet site indicated wind chills of -15 to -25 degrees Fahrenheit.
Guadalupe Pass ASOS indicated wind chills of -15 to -35 degrees Fahrenheit.
Sustained winds of 40 mph or greater occurred in Guadalupe Pass for a few hours.
Several hours of sustained westerly winds of 40 mph or greater occurred at Artesia.
An extended period of high winds occurred in the Davis Mountains as strong mid level winds at the base of a passing upper trough moved over the region.
The McDonald Observatory on Mount Locke in the Davis Mountains recorded wind chill values of -15 to -30 Fahrenheit.
Wind chill values of -15 to -20 Fahrenheit occurred.
Wind chills of -15 to -25 Fahrenheit occured at the McDonald Observatory on Mount Locke.
Wind chill values of -15 to -20 degrees Fahrenheit were observed.
The Lamesa West Texas Mesonet site recorded wind chills of -15 to -20 degrees Fahrenheit.
A ranger at Guadalupe National Park reported visibilities of less than 3/4 of a mile due to blowing dust across the region.
Blowing dust reduced visibilities to near 0 miles across the Van Horn and Highway 54 corridor.  Several vehicles were involved in an accident, due to the blowing dust, along US 90.

events.cz_name: REEVES COUNTY AND UPPER TRANS PECOS
events.event_narrative: The Reeves County Emergency Manager reported near zero mile visibility near Pecos, Texas.  Vehicles were traveling very slow across the county.
The NWS in San Angelo relayed a report of several accidents across Andrews County due to blowing dust and smoke.  An indirect fatality was reported with one of the accidents.

At 8:55 PM CST, the broadcast media reported several cars were under water on the west side of Big Spring.  About an hour later, the Big Spring Police Department reported several streets were closed due to high water crossing roadways.
The hail almost covered the ground.
Named the Bate's Field Fire, this fire burned 3200 acres and threatened 300 homes, a power plant and a water treatment plant.
A fire, known as the Texland Fire, occurred in Andrews County and burned 8,000 acres.  Four structures were threatened and saved.
A fire, known as the Sand Ranch Fire, burned 5,000 acres in Andrews County.  Numerous structures, oil wells, and tank batteries were threatened and saved.
A fire, known as the Turner Fire, burned 3,200 acres in Midland County.  Several oil pump jacks and other oil field equipment was threatened and saved.
The fire, known as the Sanderson Fire, burned 3,590 acres in Terrell County.  One Sheffield volunteer fire department firefighter was injured and 4 structures were threatened.

This fire was known as the Rockhouse Fire.  It burned 314,444 acres in Jeff Davis and Presidio Counties in west Texas.  It may have started from an electrical problem in an abandoned building near Marfa, TX.  This fire destroyed 41 homes, 2 businesses, 150 cattle, 15 calves, 9 horses, 30 fences, and 100-200 power poles.  Despite the damage, 260 homes were reported to be saved.  The fire was reported to be the largest in history for the state of Texas, and it was finally contained on 5/12/2011 around 3 PM CST.
A fire, known as the Hickman Fire, started in Midland County and burned 16,500 acres.  Thirty-four homes and 5 outbuildings were destroyed.  Five hundred people were evacuated.
A complex of fires, known as the Cannon Fire, burned 63,427 acres in Pecos County.
A fire, known as the Frying Pan Ranch, burned 80,907 acres in Andrews County.  Numerous homes were threatened by this fire, but all structures were reportedly saved.
A fire, known as the Fuller Ranch Fire, burned 5,200 acres in Scurry County.

A fire, known as the Roper Fire, burned 41,000 acres in Brewster County.  Several structures were threatened, but saved.  The fire was started from someone throwing a cigarette on the ground at a roping event at the Sul Ross State University SALE Arena in Alpine, TX.

This fire, known as the Pleasant Farms Fire, burned 4,000 acres in Ector County.  Several homes were threatened, and one home was destroyed.  This fire eventually merged with the C-Bar fire in Crane County.
This fire, known as the C-Bar Fire, burned 13,000 acres in Crane County.  This fire merged with the Pleasant Farms fire in Ector County.
This fire, known as the Champion Fire, burned 1,000 acres in Mitchell County.  Six homes were threatened and saved.  Three homes were destroyed.
This fire, known as the Schwartz Fire, burned 83,000 acres in Brewster County.  Two structures were threatened and saved.  Sixteen structures were indirectly threatened.
The fire, known as the Gage Holland Fire, burned about 6,000 acres.  Forty Homes were threatened, and one home under construction was destroyed.
This fire, known as the Iron Mountain Fire, burned 80,000 acres in Brewster County.
This fire, known as the Matt Loop Fire, burned 1,291 acres in Howard County near Big Spring, TX.  Four homes were destroyed, and thirty homes were threatened.  Sixty homes were evacuated.

This fire, known as the Price Fire, burned 3,373 acres in Glasscock County.  Fifty pump jacks, twelve or more tank batteries, and one home were threatened and saved.  Miles of polypipe and utility poles were burned.
This fire, known as the CEED fire, burned 5,000 acres in Midland County.  The fire was six miles long, and crossed Loop 250 in the City of Midland.
This fire, known as the Derick Fire, burned around 25,000 acres in Andrews County and moved into portions of Martin County.  The fire destroyed 110 power poles.
This fire in Winkler County burned 9,600 acres.  One firefighter received burn injuries and was flown to the burn center in Lubbock, TX.

Tornado damage was reported near Sanderson at approximately 17:45 CST.  Several cedar trees were destroyed as the tornado tracked east southeast.  A home and barn were also destroyed by the tornado.  Spotter reports indicate the tornado was 1/2 mile wide and travelled approximately 9 miles.
Sustained northeast winds of 40 mph or greater occurred for 3 hours in Guadalupe Pass behind a cold front.
Several hours of sustained westerly winds over 40 mph occurred in the Guadalupe Mountains.
Sustained westerly winds of 40 mph or greater occurred in the Guadalupe Mountains for more than two hours.
This report was relayed by the local radio station.  Minor damage to tree limbs was also reported.
Several tree limbs were snapped by strong wind gusts, in addition to an 18 wheel cattle trailer being blown over.  The size of the tree limbs was unknown.
The hail covered the ground.
The hail covered the ground.
The time of this report was estimated based on radar data.
The park ranger's windshield was broken by the hail.
High winds were also reported, although an estimate for the speed was not available.

A COOP Observer reported a downburst moved through Lajitas sometime between 1800-1830 CST.  The wind damaged the roofs of some structures, although the type of these roofs was not available in the report.
An estimated 20 to 30 power poles were knocked down or damaged along SH 17.
One foot of water was reported flowing over SH 166, 6 miles southwest of Fort Davis.

Power poles and trees were blown down.  The tree sizes and number of power poles/trees were unknown.  Power outages were also reported just west of Colorado City, TX.  The property damage for this event was estimated.
Sustained winds of 40 mph or greater occurred through Guadalupe Pass for no less than fourteen consecutive hours.
Four inches of snowfall was reported 2 miles southwest of Knapp, which is approximately 14 miles west/southwest of Snyder.

Four inches of snowfall was reported in Lenorah, which is located approximately 6 miles east of Tarzan.  Thunderstorms aided a rapid phase change to snow with the heaviest snowfall occurring after the precipitation changeover.

Snowfall mixed with sleet late on the 22nd until early on the 23rd, before changing to all snow.  Snowfall of 3+ inches was reported in Hope at 735 AM CST on the 23rd along with icy roads.  The final snow total at Hope was 12 inches reported at 922 AM CST on the 24th.

Snow began during the eveing of the 22nd, and fell through the night with 3-4 inches reported on the ground in Carlsbad the morning of December 23rd.  The temperature was in the upper 20s.  Snowfall continued nearly unabated through the day on the 23rd and 24th with a storm total of 12-14 inches.  The Carlsbad ASOS (KCNM) had the snow beginning at roughly the same time the storm spotters reported.

Roads became snow packed and icy around Artesia by 835 AM CST on the 23rd, although snowfall totals were only 1-2 inches.  Snowfall persisted through the day and night with Artesia ending up with a total of 9.5 inches which was reported at 11:16 AM CST on the 24th.

Several hours of moderate snow fell before freezing rain mixed with the snow early on the 23rd.  Since temperatures were in the 20s through the evening on the 22nd, and considering the moderate snowfall, several inches of snowfall were possible along with icy roads.  Snow continued through the day and night on the 23rd and ended late in the morning on the 24th with 17 inches total.
The Queen Fire Department reported a total of 7 inches of snowfall.

Snowfall totals were great enough by 714 PM CST on the 23rd over east central New Mexico for Highway 18 to be closed between Hobbs and Lovington.  There were injuries from several automobile accidents reported.   US Highway 62/180 between Hobbs and Carlsbad was closed by 825 PM CST.  Law enforcement was working an accident on US 82 west of Lovington at that time also.  Total snowfall at Hobbs was 7 inches.

Snowfall was only 1-2 inches by early evening on the 23rd, however roads began to be closed over Lea County due to snowfall and subfreezing temperatures.  The storm total snowfall reported for Tatum was 8 inches.
Storm total snowfall at Jal was 4 inches.
Seminole spotter reported a total of 6 inches of snowfall.
Storm total snowfall for Mentone was 6-8 inches.
The spotter reported nickel hail almost covered the ground.
Minor fence damage was reported.  The time of this report was estimated based on other hail reports and radar data.
The time of this report was estimated according to radar data.  No damage was reported with the hail.
Law enforcement reported wind gusts near 60 mph and near zero visibility due to blowing dust in Carlsbad, NM.
Andrews had a total of 5 inches of snowfall.
Kermit reported 4-6 inches of total snowfall.

Several car wrecks were reported in Midland by the Midland County Emergency Manager's office at 1835 CST, including a 5 vehicle wreck.  No injury reports were received.  The EM's office also reported an inch of snow at that time.  A total of 6.4 inches of snowfall was recorded at the NWS office at Midland International Airport.
The total snowfall at Lenorah, which is located approximately 6 miles east of Tarzan, was 6 inches.
Odessa had a total of 4-6 inches of snowfall.
Greenwood, which is approximately 10 miles east of Midland, reported a total of 4.3 inches of snowfall.
Considering Pine Springs in the Guadalupe Mountains had 17 inches of snowfall, northern portions of the Van Horn and Highway 54 corridor zone could have had 8-10 inches of snowfall.
Five inches of snow reported in Fort Stockton.
Five and two tenths of an inch of snowfall reported in Kermit.
Four inches of snow reported in Midland.  The total was up to 5 inches at 1400 CST.
Six inches of snowfall reported in Greenwood, or 10.8 miles east of Midland.  A total of 10.1 inches was reported by 0545 CST on 1/10/12 in Greenwood.
Five inches of snowfall reported in Andrews.
Estimated 4 inches of snowfall by 1200 CST, but the total snowfall was 6 inches by 1420 CST.
A total of 10.6 inches of snow fell at the NWS Midland office.
Estimated 4 inches of snow fell by 1200 CST in Nadine, which is 7.8 miles south of Hobbs.  The total snowfall was 15 inches, which was reported at 1900 CST.
Four inches of snowfall was reported in Queen by 0500 CST on 1/9/12.
A total of 7 inches of snow fell in northeastern Reagan county, approximately 25 miles north-northeast of Big Lake.
A total of 8-10 inches of snowfall was estimated in western Glasscock County.
A total of 9-10 inches of snowfall was estimated over Martin County.
A total of 7-9 inches of snowfall was estimated over southwestern Dawson County.
A total of 9 inches of snowfall was reported in Seminole.
A total of 4 inches of snowfall was estimated in Big Spring.
A total of 4 inches of snowfall was estimated over southwestern Scurry County.
A total of 4 inches of snowfall was estimated in northeastern Mitchell County.
A total of 8-9 inches of snowfall was estimated over northern Crane County.
A total of 8-9 inches of snowfall was estimated over northern Upton County.
A total of 6-7 inches was estimated over notheastern Loving County.
A total of 8-9 inches of snowfall was estimated in eastern Ward County.

events.cz_name: REEVES COUNTY AND UPPER TRANS PECOS
events.event_narrative: A total of 4-5 inches of snowfall was estimated over eastern Reeves County.
A total of 4-5 inches of snowfall was estimated in southern Lea county.
A total of 6-7 inches of snowfall was estimated over southwestern Borden County.
Sustained northeast winds of 45-51 mph occurred in Guadalupe Pass for 4 consecutive hours.
Sustained northeast winds of 40-44 mph occurred in Guadalupe Pass.
Several gusts over 60 mph occurred in the higher elevations of the Guadalupe Mountains.
An extended period of strong winds affected the Guadalupe Mountains.
An extended period of strong winds affected the Guadalupe Mountains.
Several hours of strong wind gusts affected the higher elevations of the Guadalupe Mountains.
Strong wind gusts affected the Guadalupe Mountains over a several hour period.

Strong winds affected the higher elevations of the guadalupe mountains during a 24 hour period.  The strongest winds were in the higher elevations of the Guadalupes where gusts ranged from 58 mph to 92 mph for the duration.
Strong wind gusts occurred for at least one hour in Artesia.  Received a report of a tree falling on a carport and vehicle.
Strong winds were recorded at McDonald Observatory on Mount Locke in the Davis Mountains.
The roof on an airplane hangar collapsed at the time of these higher winds.
Several high wind gusts occurred at Carlsbad.
Strong wind gusts occurred in McKittrick Canyon.
Several strong wind gusts occurred in Alpine.
The public reported a tornado approximately 20 miles south of Ft. Stockton, west of Highway 285.  Photos of the tornado were sent to CBS 7 via Facebook.  No damage was reported with this tornado.

This event location was estimated based on public reports, photos, and radar data.  CBS 7 has photos of this tornado available on their Facebook page.  No damage was reported with this tornado.  It is unclear whether or not this tornado continued its path into Terrell County, where another tornado was reported (with damage) a little over an hour later.
Northeast winds of 40 to 46 mph occurred for an extended period of time through Guadalupe Pass.
An extended period of strong winds affected the Guadalupe Mountains due to the passage of an upper shortwave trough.
An extended period of strong winds affected the Guadalupe Mountains due to a passing upper shortwave trough.

A line of severe thunderstorms moved into Ector County around 11:20 PM CDT March 18th and progressed eastward.  At 12:28 AM CDT March 19th, a tornado touched down in the Gardendale community and remained on the ground for two minutes.  This tornado produced damage along County Road 30 (Goldenrod Drive) primarily between Chinaberry Avenue and Alfalfa Avenue.  As the tornado developed, it moved just south of an RV Park located near the intersection of County Road 30 and China Berry Ave.  This resulted in a large camper being toppled by severe northwest winds flowing into the tornado.  One minor injury was noted at this location.  As the tornado intensified and progressed northeastward, strong inflow winds from the south resulted in a cinder block fence being blown over to the north.  Finally, as the tornado crossed County Road 30 (Goldenrod Drive), it reached its peak intensity.  This resulted in significant damage to a residential home, along with a 20' x 30' travel trailer and a barn being destroyed.  Widespread damage was noted in this area, which also served as a collection point for a great amount of debris from other locations upwind back to the southwest.  South of County Road 30, power poles with broken cross members were noted.  This was indicative of EF1 tornado damage.  However, the tornado intensified after crossing to the north side of County Road 30 (Goldenrod Drive).  There was a home that shifted slightly off its foundation.  Also, there was significant loss of roof decking and major shingle loss.  Some small pieces of debris became projectiles, sticking into the walls of the home.  Based on this information, winds for this event were estimated to be 90-110 mph.   The Gardendale tornado at its most intense - north of County Road 30 - was rated as a low end EF-2 tornado.
Sustained winds of 40-43 mph, and a gust to 55 mph, occurred at the Artesia Airport for several hours.
Sustained west winds of 40-41 mph, and a gust to 55 mph, occurred through Guadalupe Pass for several hours.
Several hours of high winds occurred in Guadalupe Pass, with gusts as high as 66 mph.
A period of high sustained winds of 40-43 mph occurred at the Batdraw RAWS site behind a strong cold front, with a gust to 57 mph.
A period of high winds of 40-44 mph occurred over portions of the southeast New Mexico Plains behind a strong cold front.
The passage of a strong cold front resulted in high winds of 40-47 mph sustained over a several hour period through Guadalupe Pass.  Several gusts of 50-55 mph also occurred during this time.
High winds also occurred in the higher elevations of the Guadalupe Mountains.  Sustained winds around 40 mph, and gusts around 60 mph, were registered for 4 hours.
A 1-2 hour period of high winds around 40 mph sustained occurred at the Artesia Automated Surface Observing System.  A gust to 54 mph was reported during this time.
A 1-2 hour period of high winds around 40 mph sustained occurred at the Carlsbad Automated Surface Observing System.  A gust of 50 mph was reported during this time.
An extended period of high sustained winds of 41-64 mph, and gusts of 58-75 mph, occurred in the Guadalupe Mountains.
An extensive period of high winds affected the higher elevations of the Guadalupe Mountains.  Sporadic high wind gusts of 59-62 mph occurred during this time.
Showers and virga over the area resulted in a dry microburst with winds over 65 mph in downtown Midland. This caused a sign on top of a fourteen story building to be damaged.
A thunderstorm moved over Crane County and produced a wind gust of 65 mph four miles west of Crane.
A storm moved over Mitchell County and produced half dollar sized hail and winds over 60 mph six miles south southeast of Colorado City.
A storm moved over Mitchell County and produced three inch hail thirteen miles south of Westbrook.  A rotating wall cloud was reported with this storm.

A storm moved over Reagan County and produced at least quarter sized hail twenty-five miles north northeast of Big Lake.  A COOP observer reported a fifteen inch hail drift with quarter sized hail present about 24 hours after the storm. Leaves were stripped off the trees.
A storm moved over Reagan County and produced golfball sized hail and wind speeds over 60 mph nine miles southeast of Stiles.
A line of storms moved through Reagan County and produced golfball sized hail and 60 mph winds in Big Lake.  The trained spotter reported tree branches on the ground.

A thunderstorm moved through Eddy County and produced half dollar sized hail in Malaga.  The hail covered the ground and caused cracks in a windshield and dents on a truck.  The cost for the damage to the vehicles is a rough estimate.
A severe thunderstorm produced tennis ball sized hail seven miles north of Orla.  Winds between 50 and 60 mph occured on State Road 25.

At 3:21 pm CDT, a trained spotter positioned along Highway 90 between Marfa and Alpine witnessed the development of a funnel cloud.  At 3:24 pm CDT, the funnel appeared to develop a wall cloud.  At 3:30 pm CDT, debris was clearly indicated extending east of Paisano Pass.  From another spotter looking at the storm, the tornado appeared to move southwest during its life cycle.  The tornado did not seem to last more than four minutes before dissipating at approximately 3:34 pm CDT.  The tornado was rated as an EF-O.

A thunderstorm moved across Ector County and produced wind damage in Odessa.  The wind damage was determined to be from a microburst.  The most intense winds and greatest damage during the thunderstorm was confined to Triple Crown Drive near the intersection of South Gallant Fox Avenue in Odessa.  Damage consisted of a corrugated tin roof partially blown off of a barn.  A side addition to the barn collapsed from the wind.  Tree branches of up to two inches from a partially live tree were broken.  Debris from the barn roof travelled about 200 yards across the street and punctured a mobile home.  Winds also blew off part of the siding from the mobile home.  A vehicle on the property was damaged by the wind and the roof debris.  The West Odessa Fire Department reported several power poles snapped in the area.  Based on the damage, the peak wind speed was 70 to 80 mph.  The cost of damage is a very rough estimate.

Law enforcement officials reported mud and rock slides on portions of U.S. Highway 180/62.  The cost of damage is a very rough estimate.

The cost of damage is a very rough estimate since the number of cars and homes affected is unknown and the extent of the damage is unknown.
Sustained northeast winds of 40-46 mph occurred for 16 hours through Guadalupe Pass.
Strong winds also occurred in the higher elevations of the Guadalupe Mountains.
Sporadic high winds occurred through the day in the Guadalupe Mountains.

Light freezing rain, sleet and snow fell beginning on the morning of 11/22/13.  The light mix continued through the day and overnight.  Heavier precipitation consisting of snow, sleet and freezing rain fell the night of 11/23-11/24 with 3.2 inches of snow, sleet and freezing rain reported on the morning of 11/24.  Portions of Highway 62/180 closed due to icy roads to the southwest of Carlsbad.

A mix of freezing rain, sleet and snow began on the morning of 12/22.  Accumulations were light through the day and the night of 11/22-11/23.  Heavier precipitation fell the night of 11/23-11/24, with snow being the main precipitation type.  4 inches of snow was reported by 530 am MST in Cottonwood near Artesia.

Light freezing rain and sleet fell from the morning of 11/22 until the afternoon of 11/23.  However, heavier freezing rain fell the evening of 11/23 with a 1/4 inch of ice accumulation by 953 pm CST.  Over 60 car wrecks were reported in Midland from the morning of 11/22 to the morning of 11/24.  Numerous roads closed, particularly Loop 250 in Midland.  There were no fatalities, and several injuries, none serious.  Power lines down due to icing with 3,167 meters still out as of 6 pm CST 11/24.  Each meter represents a residence or business.

A mix of light freezing rain and snow fell from the morning of 11/22 through the day and night.  More freezing rain fell during the day on 11/23 with 2 inches of sleet and snow the night of 11/23-11/24.
The Winkler County S.O. reported 1/4 inch to 1 inch ice accumulation due to freezing rain.  A little sleet and snow mixed in at times.
The Crane County S.O. reported 1/4 to 1/2 inch ice accumulation due to a mix of freezing rain, sleet and snow.   Roads are icy.
The Andrews County S.O. reported around an inch of ice accumulation due to freezing rain and a little sleet.
The Gaines County S.O. reported very icy roads across Gaines County, but no estimate on ice accumulation.  Amounts up and downstream indicate at least 1/4 inch of ice accumulation.

The Ector County S.O. reported up to 2 inches of ice accumulation.  A tractor trailer slid off Interstate 20 approximately 13 miles southwest of Odessa.  Overpasses on Interstate 20 closed from 10 to 13 miles southwest of Odessa due to icing.  As of 6 pm CST on 11/24, 2,188 meters were still out in Odessa due to power lines down from icing.  Each meter represents a residence or business.

The Upton County S.O. reported an inch ice accumulation from a mix of freezing rain and sleet, but mainly freezing rain.  Two cars slid off the road in Rankin.  No injuries reported.  At least 100 people without electricity due to downed power lines from icing.
The Dawson County S.O. reported about 1/4 inch of ice accumulation.
The Loving county S.O. reported ice accumulation up to an inch due to a mix of freezing rain and sleet.

events.cz_name: REEVES COUNTY AND UPPER TRANS PECOS
events.event_narrative: The Reeves County S.O. reported 1/4 inch of ice accumulation from a mix of freezing rain, sleet and snow.

The Culberson County S.O. reported over 1/4 inch of ice accumulation.  Portions of Highway 90 south of Van Horn closed due to icing.  Power went out around 4 am CST on 11/24 due to power lines down from icing.  The Rio Grande Electric Power Co. reported many power poles down in Culberson County.  The weight of the ice dragged the lines down, which then had a domino effect on the power poles.

Icy roads reported by the Culberson County S.O.  The Guadalupe Pass ASOS reported nearly an inch of ice accumulation on the freezing rain sensor before the sensor went out for lack of power.  Rio Grande Electric Coop reported 494 power poles down due to icing in Dell City, with 205 still to be replaced as of 12/12/13.  438 meters are still out of power as of 12/12/13.

The public reported 1/2 inch of ice accumulation and icy roads, 3 miles southwest of Big Spring.  The Howard County S.O. reported an inch of ice accumulation in Big Spring, icy roads and a wreck on Interstate 20, 15 miles east of Big Spring at 921 am CST.
At 852 am CST 11/24, The DPS reported many vehicles stranded on Interstate 20 for 4-5 hours due to icy conditions.

The DPS reported Loop 250 in Midland and Highway 191 between Midland and Odessa closed due to icy roads.  Three tractor trailers wrecked 5.5 miles east of Midland in the west bound lane of Interstate 20 due to icy roads.  Another wreck was reported on Interstate 20 on the Ector/Midland county line.  The Midland P.D. responded to 5 major wrecks the evening of 11/23 within 2 hours.  No fatalities were reported, but some minor injuries.
The Martin County S.O. reported ice accumulation of about 1 inch.  At 8 am CST 11/24, the S.O. reported a rollover in Stanton due to icy roads.

The Borden County S.O. reported icy roads from freezing rain and a little sleet, but no accumulation estimated.  According to up and downstream ice accumulations, approximately 1/4 inch of ice accumulated in Borden County.
The Glasscock County S.O. reported 2-3 inches of ice accumulation.  Power lines were down across the county due to heavy icing.

The Pecos County S.O. reported 1/4 inch of ice accumulation.  Portions of a 5 mile stretch of road were closed on Interstate 10 due to icy conditions, 3 miles east of Fort Stockton.  Rio Grande Electric Coop reported 152 power poles down in Fort Stockton due to icing, with 12 still to be replaced as of 12/12/13.  114 meters were still out of power as of 12/12/13.

The Reagan County S.O. reported 1/2 inch ice accumulation from a mix of freezing rain and sleet.  Roads were icy and power lines were reported down across the county.  At least 100 people were without power due to downed power lines.

The Scurry County S.O. reported 1/4-1/2 inch of ice accumulation from a mix of freezing rain and sleet.  Roads are icy and power outages have occurred in Snyder the night of 11/23-11/24 and this morning, 11/24.
The Mitchell county S.O. reported 1/4 inch ice accumulation from a mix of freezing rain and sleet.  Several accidents reported on Interstate 20 in and near Colorado City and Loraine.
The Terrell Gas Plant in northern Terrell County reported 1/4-1/2 inch of ice accumulation.  Roads were icy in the morning, but the ice melted by noon CST on 11/24.

The Presidio County S.O. reported 1/4-1/2 inch of ice accumulation from a mix of freezing rain and sleet, mainly freezing rain.  Accidents reported on Highway 90 between Marfa and Alpine, and on Highway 67 between Presidio and Marfa due to icy roads.  4, 849 people were without power in Marfa, Alpine, Valentine, Fort Davis and Marathon.

The Presidio County S.O. reported icy roads in Fort Davis, but no estimate on ice accumulation.  The power went out in Fort Davis on the evening of 11/23 due to downed power lines.  1/4 inch ice estimated from locations up and downstream. 4, 849 people were without power in Marfa, Alpine, Valentine, Fort Davis and Marathon.  Rio Grande Electric Coop reported 300 power poles down in Alpine, with 17 more to replace as of  12/12/13.  129 meters were still out in the Alpine area by 12/12/13.

Law enforcement reported 1/2 inch ice accumulation on roads in and near Marathon.  Power outages in Marathon, Alpine and south of Alpine.  4, 849 people were without power in Marfa, Alpine, Valentine, Fort Davis and Marathon.
Public reported 3.8 inches of snowfall and 1/2 inch of ice in Tatum.
Lea County S.O. reported 1/4 ice accumulation, in addition to 2 inches of sleet and snow.
The Eddy County S.O. reported 1/4 inch of ice accumulation.  Portions of Highway 62/180 closed due to ice to the southwest of Carlsbad.
The Ward County S.O. reported 1/4 inch of ice from a mix of freezing rain and sleet.  Roads were icy.
A quarter inch of ice accumulation reported in Jal.  Freezing rain on the 5th was followed by sleet the night of the 5th and morning of the 6th.

It is unclear at this time whether the accident is in Pecos County or Brewster County, and no word of any fatalities at this time.

A thunderstorm moved across Mitchell County and produced a tornado in Loraine.  A damage survey was conducted the next day.  The tornado touched down at approximately 9 am CDT and continued generally northeast for a distance of 0.16 miles before lifting.  The tornado was on the ground for less than one minute.  There was extensive damage to a barn where several walls collapsed and a pole with a cement base was pulled out of the ground.  There was also damage to the local fire chief's house where debris from the barn became embedded in the side of the house.  At its widest the tornado was estimated to have a width of approximately 50 yards.  Based on the damage, the tornado will be rated as an EF-1 with estimated wind speeds of 100 mph.  The cost of damage is a very rough estimate.

A thunderstorm moved across Howard County and produced a tornado near Big Spring.  Eyewitness reports from storm chasers and spotters in the area indicate that the tornado began at 6:13 pm CDT just south of Texas State Highway 176, approximately 10 miles west of Big Spring.  The tornado then moved southeastward over open fields, bounded by Natural Dam Lake to its west and Wilkinson Road just to its east.  The tornado continued on this southeast track along Salt Lake, eventually crossing Interstate 20 at approximately 6:32 pm CDT.  ||South of Interstate 20, the tornado exhibited erratic movement, being described by chasers and spotters as being nearly stationary in a field.  Examination of radar imagery showed the primary storm circulation moved slowly southeastward to approximately half a mile northwest of the intersection of Lintner Road and Rockhouse Road by 6:37 pm CDT, before turning eastward.  The tornado continued to move east, with the southern periphery of the tornado affecting Home #1.  The tornado then began to move northeastward, crossing nearly directly over Home #2 around 6:40 pm CDT.  A slight east northeast turn allowed for only the tornado's northern periphery to affect Home #3 along Cauble Road around 6:42 pm CDT.||The tornado moved southward along or near Cauble Road.  The tornado continued its erratic behavior, moving southwestward and re-entering the same field as previous around 6:48 pm CDT.  The tornado then turned west-northwestward, eventually becoming quasi-stationary just east of the Home #1 between 6:52 pm and 6:54 pm CDT, before moving westward, just north of Home #1.  Residents at home #1 described how long the tornado lasted and felt the tornado had impacted them twice. The tornado dissipated approximately 1.5 miles west of Home #1 around 7 pm CDT.||The damage assessment team looked at several different indicators to determine tornado intensity.  At Home #2, which likely was the closest and strongest structure to the tornado during the most intense portion of the tornado's life cycle, the entire roof was destroyed and exterior walls on this well-constructed residence were partially collapsed.  This damage indicator suggests an EF-3 intensity with wind speeds estimated at 140-160 mph.  In the adjacent field east of Home #2, a 640 type pump jack was blown over.  The assessment team also looked at tree damage at Home #2.  Both softwood and hardwood trees were viewed on the property.  Damage to these large trees was indicative of high end EF-2 to low end EF-3 damage.||Home #1 and Home #3 experienced tornado damage indicative of EF-2 damage.  In the examples shown, large sections of the roof were removed, but with the walls still standing.  At Home #3, there were power poles that were snapped approximately five feet off the ground.  Wind speeds at this residence are estimated at 115 to 125 mph.  At Home #1, trees were uprooted.  Wind speeds are estimated at this location of 105 to 115 mph.  The cost of damage from this tornado is a very rough estimate.

This tornado developed at around 6:51 pm CDT, approximately three miles south of the interstate, close to Farm-to-Market Road 818.  This tornado was anticyclonic and moved slowly east and then northeast.  With the help of radar imagery, it is estimated that the tornado lasted 8 minutes, while traveling a path just short of 2 miles.  With the tornado remaining over open fields, the assessment team rated the tornado as an EF0.  The width was estimated at 100 yards.

The tornado traveled a 2.3 mile path, moving westward.  The tornado dissipated approximately four miles northwest of Lees at 7:28 pm CDT.  Without damage indicators, the tornado is rated as an EF-0 with an estimated width of 100 yards.

A thunderstorm moved across Glasscock County and produced a tornado near Lees, TX.  This tornado developed around 7:38 pm CDT approximately four miles southeast of Lomax.  This short-lived tornado traveled a distance of approximately a half of a mile, dissipating by 7:40 pm CDT.  With no damage indicators, this tornado is rated as an EF-0 with an estimated path length of 50 yards.

A thunderstorm moved across Glasscock County and produced a tornado near Lees, TX.  This tornado developed at 7:55 pm CDT, approximately four miles southwest of Lees, north of Hillger Road.  The tornado, estimated at 200 yards wide, snapped 14 power poles along Hillger Road as it moved slowly southeast.  With the poles being snapped approximately five feet off the ground, wind speeds were estimated at about 115 mph, indicating a lower-end EF-2 tornado intensity.  There was also a nearby metal building just south of Hillger Road which sustained a loss of metal roof panels due to the tornado.  Wind speeds at this location were estimated at 90-100 mph, indicating EF-1 intensity.  As it weakened in intensity, this slow moving tornado made an abrupt turn to the northeast and dissipated at 8:07 pm CDT near the intersection of Hillger Road and Ranch Road 33.  The cost of damage is a very rough estimate.

A thunderstorm moved across Glasscock County and produced a tornado near Garden City.  This tornado developed just west of Ranch Road 33, four miles north northwest of Garden City around 8:42 pm CDT.  The tornado moved southward, knocking over a 640 type pump jack located approximately two and a quarter miles north of Garden City.  This type of occurrence is associated with wind speeds in the 140-160 mph range.  Thus, the tornado has been rated as briefly reaching EF-3 intensity.  Broken tree limbs were observed by the assessment team two miles north of Garden City, just west of Ranch Road 33.  This damage indicator suggested the tornado had weakened to EF-1 intensity at that point.  This weakening trend coincided with the tornado taking a more southeast track as it crossed Ranch Road 33.  The tornado dissipated at 8:54 pm CDT, two miles north of Garden City.  In total, the tornado traveled a 3.7 mile path and had an estimated width of 200 yards.  The cost of damage is a very rough estimate.

A thunderstorm moved across Glasscock County and produced a tornado near Garden City.  This tornado developed around 8:56 pm CDT, just over 1.5 miles north northwest of Garden City.  This tornado produced a combination of EF-1 and EF-2 damage at two residences.  A single-wide manufactured home at Home #1 was rolled and destroyed.  This was indicative of damage produced by a tornado of EF-2 intensity.  As the tornado moved southwestward and impacted Home #2, a combination of EF-1 and EF-2 damage was noted.  Tree damage was indicative of EF-1, while the metal barn appears to have sustained lower-end EF-2 damage.  It is noted however that the barn construction made it more susceptible to wind entering the structure, which could have resulted in damage at a lower wind threshold.  Wind speeds are estimated at 100-115 mph with this damage.||As the tornado moved southwestward, it was the opinion of the assessment team that the tornado intensified.  At approximately 9:01 pm CDT, the tornado knocked over a 320 type pump jack west of County Road 417.  With this slightly smaller pump jack type, it was felt that winds in the 120-135 mph range could potentially produce this damage.  Thus, the tornado was rated as being a high-end EF-2 intensity.  Oil field workers noted that there was damage over open fields farther to the southwest.  Using radar estimates, the team concluded that this tornado dissipated at 9:02 pm CDT just short of reaching Highway 158, 1.5 miles west of Garden City.  The total path length for tornado #7 was 1.9 miles with its greatest width estimated at 150 yards.  The cost of damage is a very rough estimate.

A supercell thunderstorm developed over Andrews County during the evening hours of September 17th.  This storm encountered a stationary boundary and began moving southeast.  The storm began to form a hook echo at 6:30 pm CDT as it moved toward Highway 115 in southwest Andrews County.  Eyewitness reports from storm chasers and spotters in the area indicate that the initial tornado began at 7:13 pm CDT near the intersection of Andrews, Winkler and Ector Counties.  Videos taken of the tornado show it touching down and lifting several times before eventually staying on the ground for several minutes over far northwest portions of Ector County.  The tornado moved south southeastward across open fields of rural Ector County just west of FM 181.  The damage assessment team looked at several different indicators to determine tornado intensity.  The tornado snapped several electrical power poles and overturned a tank battery along its path.  These damage indicators suggest EF1 intensity with wind speeds estimated at 90 to 105 mph.  Near the end of the life cycle of the EF1 tornado, a weak anticyclonic circulation developed on the forward flank of the supercell around 7:25 pm CDT.  This circulation moved southwest to the west of FM 181 and dissipated around 7:35 pm CDT. Storm chasers and spotters identified this funnel looking north from Goldsmith around 7:30 pm CDT.  There was no evidence of damage or reports of the funnel cloud touching down.  The tornado path width was estimated and the cost of damage is a very rough estimate.

Trained spotters viewed and took images of a tornado that developed two miles east of the community of Midkiff along Farm to Market Road 2401 and continued northeastward into open fields in extreme southwest portions of Glasscock County. A tornado formed along Farm to Market Road 2401. The tornado was narrow, 50 to 75 yards wide, and moved almost parallel and just south of FM 2401 during a 1.8 mile stretch before weakening somewhere near Highway 137. A small barn or outbuilding was destroyed by the tornado at approximately 7:28 pm. One wall of the structure remained. This type of damage is indicative of EF-1 damage with winds of approximately 100 to 110 mph. Pieces of the metal roof were blown northeastward across FM 2401 into an open field. Two silos/storage tanks were also displaced from their original locations. There was a stretch of 32 power poles that were snapped off within a few feet of the ground which is indicative of low-end EF-2 damage. Wind speeds necessary to produce this type of damage are estimated at around 120 mph. This tornado was rated as an EF-2. The cost of the damage is a very rough estimate.

High winds were reported across the Guadalupe Mountains, Saturday morning and afternoon.  A 66 mph peak wind was reported at the Guadalupe Bowl during the mid morning.
High wind gusts occurred at Guadalupe Pass on Monday afternoon.  Additional high winds were observed late Monday into the early morning hours on Tuesday.
High winds were reported at McDonald Observatory during the afternoon on Monday, January 7.

High winds briefly occurred at the Guadalupe Bowl Wednesday afternoon, with a 60 mph wind gust reported during this time.  High winds were again measured late Wednesday night and early Thursday morning, with a peak wind of 69 mph around midnight.
High winds were measured at McDonald Observatory, beginning just prior to midnight, late Wednesday night.  These high winds continued for approximately two hours before gradually diminishing.
Winds increased during the overnight hours, early Sunday morning.  A peak wind of 59 mph was measured at Guadalupe Pass around 2 am MST.
Northeast winds behind a cold front gusted to above high wind criteria during the morning hours of January 16.
Sustained winds late Wednesday into the early morning hours on Thursday reached high wind criteria.  A peak sustained wind of 45 mph was reported just before midnight at Guadalupe Pass.
Winds briefly gusted above high wind criteria at Guadalupe Pass during the afternoon of January 21.
Sustained northeast winds of 40-45 mph persisted through Guadalupe Pass for a good portion of the morning hours.

High winds across the Guadalupe Mountains lasted in excess of one day, beginning early Monday and concluding Tuesday morning.  A peak wind of 82 mph was reported at Guadalupe Bowl early Tuesday morning.  A peak wind gust of 63 mph was reported at the Pinery on Monday evening.
High winds occurred at McDonald Observatory from Monday evening through Tuesday afternoon.  Wind gusts of 65-70 mph were consistently measured throughout the event.
High winds developed in Carlsbad during the early afternoon on Monday, January 28.
High winds developed in Carlsbad early Tuesday morning.

High winds developed across the Guadalupe Mountains during the late afternoon and into the early evening hours.  The ASOS equipment at Guadalupe Pass measured a peak wind of 71 mph.  The RAWS station at the Pinery measured a peak gust of 59 mph, while the Bowl reported a wind gust of 63 mph.

McDonald Observatory experienced a prolonged high wind event.  Sustained winds of 40-45 mph along with gusts around 60 mph were common throughout the event that began Wednesday afternoon and continued into Thursday morning.

A thunderstorm moved across Eddy County and produced a tornado south of Malaga. Based on radar imagery, the tornado appeared to develop just west of U.S. Highway 285, approximately two to three miles south of Malaga and progressed northeast.  The exact path could not be determined during a survey due to the tornado���s containment within private lands, without roads to access the potential path. With insufficient|ground information, the wooden electric power poles along Highway 285 were the only|damage indicators available to assess tornado intensity. Based on radar information, it|appears the Malaga tornado formed at approximately 6:08 pm MDT, just southwest of the power poles on Highway 285 and lifted around 6:30 pm MDT (nearly crossing NM|Highway 128, 3 miles east of junction with NM Highway 31) covering a distance of 15 miles. Damaged power poles along Highway 285 were located slightly further south than was indicated on radar, 3.75 miles to 4.05 miles south of Malaga. This was used as a starting point. With the tornado crossing the power poles at approximately a 45-|degree angle, the width of the tornado was estimated at a half mile. Approximately ten power poles that were damaged to some degree as the tornado crossed Highway 285. The observed damage is consistent with damage of an EF2 tornado, with winds estimated at approximately 112 mph. The cost of damage is a very rough estimate.

A line of thunderstorms moved across Andrews County with small circulations called meso-vortices along this line. By 9:51 pm CDT, as the storm crossed Highway 385 south of Andrews, the presence of a hook echo was noted on radar. The survey team noted that damage extended from along County Road 2601 from SE 650 Road to SE 1000 Road, and then northeastward to just north of Hamrick Loop. The survey team also noted the majority of the damage coincided with the radar location of the meso-circulation and hook echo. The survey team determined that the damage was the result of a tornado. Damage to outbuildings, residential structures, power poles, and to a 300-foot transmission tower suggest that the most significant damage is indicative of a moderate to high end EF-1 tornado, with wind speeds estimated at 80-100 mph. The tornado was estimated to be 1/5 mile wide. Based on radar and damage information, it is believed that the tornado had a life span of 6 minutes, from approximately 9:55 pm to 10:01 pm. The cost of damage is a very rough estimate.

A thunderstorm moved across Ector County and produced a tornado southeast of Odessa. The tornado developed in Ector County approximately nine miles southeast of Odessa, northeast of the Pleasant Farms community, and moved northeastward into southwest portions of Midland County. The aerial survey of this tornado revealed a clearly defined path. Numerous power poles were broken. The survey also showed pump jacks and other oil field equipment that were toppled by the tornado. The tornado had a lifespan of 15 minutes. Based on research that occurred in association with the May 14, 2010 Notrees tornado, a tornado that also knocked down oil field pump jacks, this tornado was rated as an EF-3 tornado. The cost of damage is a very rough estimate.

The tornado moved northeastward, snapping power poles along County Road 300, and produced significant damage along County Road 1160 and Farm to Market Road 1379. The snapped power poles, the damage to two RVs along County Road 1160, and the damage to manufactured trailers along FM 1379 are all indicative of EF-2 tornado damage. The tornado lifespan was 10 minutes long with an estimated peak wind of 125 mph. The cost of damage is a very rough estimate.

A thunderstorm developed over eastern Culberson County and moved east northeast into northern Reeves County. This storm strengthened as it moved into Reeves County and produced significant damage to the Highway 285 RV Park about 15 miles southeast of Orla. It was determined by a National Weather Service survey team that damage to the RV park was the result of rear-flank downdraft winds which was a straight-line wind event. The survey team estimated the wind speeds to be 100-130 miles per hour based on damage to the RV park. This was based on damage to trailers, outbuildings, vehicles, and other structures. It was determined that the swath of damaging winds was around 300 yards wide and 0.75 miles in length. There was one major injury related to this event. The cost of damage is a very rough estimate.

A thunderstorm in Reeves County produced a tornado about eight miles west of Mentone. A National Weather Service survey team was unable to locate damage directly caused by the tornado due to poor road networks. Photos provided by the public and emergency management suggested that the tornado was significant, however due to a lack of damage indicators, the survey team was unable to determine a path and intensity. Thus, the tornado was rated an EF-U. It was estimated that the tornado traveled roughly 12 miles before lifting from storm spotter reports and radar signatures. The tornado started in Reeves County and moved east into Loving County. It lifted before reaching Highway 302 and moved just north of Mentone.

Power flashes were reported along with damage to northern portions of Barstow. The tornado snapped a utility pole before moving and hitting an RV park. Damage at the park included flipping a trailer on its side, damaging a pickup truck, and causing light damage to three other trailers. Wind speeds were estimated at 100 mph from the damage observed by the NWS survey team which helped classify the tornado as an EF-1. In addition to the damage observed by the survey team, spotters and the public provided visual evidence that a tornado occurred. The path length of the tornado was 0.47 miles and the path width was 20 yards. The cost of damage is a very rough estimate.

The NWS survey conducted by WFO Midland did confirm power pole damaged approximately 2.8 miles south of the Union community along Farm to Market Road 1609. This tornado damage was indicative of EF0 intensity. Based on radar imagery and storm speed, primary indications are that the tornado path extended to the west of Farm to Market Road 1609 for approximately 4-6 miles. The width of the tornado is estimated at 50 yards.

A tornado developed near the city of Winston. In Towle Park, large trees were uprooted. At the nearby High School, a 20x40 storage building adjacent to the school was rolled and destroyed. The new football scoreboard was also demolished. The uprooting of well established trees in Towle Park and the damage observed to the storage building at Snyder High School are indicative of EF1 tornado damage. EF1 damage was also observed along Voss Lane near the end of the Snyder tornado life cycle, where metal farm buildings sustained significant damage. Wind speeds for this tornado are estimated at 90-100 mph, which is believed to have stayed on the ground for approximately 3.5 minutes, travelling approximately 1.75 miles. The tornado width is estimated at 100 yards.|||A 59 mph wind gust from the north was measured at Winston Field at 3:05 pm. A 69 mph wind gust from the northwest was measured at the Texas Tech Mesonet station located 3 miles east of Snyder at 3:10 pm. In both cases, these wind gusts occurred after the tornadic supercell thunderstorm had already moved east of the area.

The NWS damage survey viewed images of a tornado 2.5 miles west southwest of Sparenberg along Farm to Market Road 828. Greg Morgan, local television meteorologist and spotter, provided visual confirmation of this weak tornado lasting approximately one minute. Mr. Morgan and other eyewitnesses estimated a tornado touchdown time of 3:45 pm CDT, and radar imagery confirmed this estimate.

Members of the Texas Tech Atmospheric Science Group and Greg Morgan from CBS 7 in Odessa witnessed the second tornado, which developed at 3:56 pm CDT, approximately 1.5 miles southwest of Sparenberg over open country, and continued until 4:00 pm. The tornado dissipated approximately 1.75 miles south of Sparenberg, just west of Farm to Market Road 26. No damage was found.

A thunderstorm moved across Dawson County and produced wind damage in and near Lamesa. Significant wind damage was discovered on the north and northeast sides of Lamesa, Texas. The damage swath included multiple uprooted trees, downed or leaning power poles, metal roofs/carports lifted or bent, some homes missing shingles or roof damage due to uprooted trees, and several damaged metal buildings and travel trailers. All of this damage was oriented in a northwest direction. After re-analysis of radar data and evaluation of eye-witness accounts, the damage was determined to be the result of an intense downburst that developed as an approaching outflow boundary interacted with an approaching supercell thunderstorm at roughly 7:45 pm CDT. The survey team estimated peak wind speeds to be between 110 to 120 mph. It was also determined that the overturned irrigation pivots, south of Lamesa, resulted from 70 to 80 mph winds behind the approaching outflow boundary. The total damage estimate between the thunderstorm winds and flooding is around 10 million dollars.

A thunderstorm moved across Ward County and produced wind damage south of Monahans. The damage swath included metal roofs/carports lifted or bent, downed tree branches between one to three inches in diameter, and several damaged travel trailers. The damage was generally oriented in an easterly direction. After re-analysis of radar data, the damage was determined to be the result of a microburst that occurred at approximately 9:15 pm CDT. The survey team estimated the peak wind speeds to be between 75 to 85 mph. The cost of damage is a very rough estimate.
